title: Uses of the Erotic: The Erotic as Power
description: An address delivered at the Fourth Berkshire Conference on the History of Women at Mount Holyoke on 25 August 1978, published first as a pamphlet and collected in Sister Outsider (1984): Lorde defines the erotic as a source of knowledge and power and distinguishes it from the pornographic.
plot_or_argument: Lorde begins by naming the erotic as a resource 'within each of us' that lies 'in a deeply female and spiritual plane' and that has been made suspect: women have been taught that the erotic is a sign of the inferior, the animal or the merely sexual, and the result is that the power attached to it has been surrendered. She distinguishes the erotic from the pornographic with the neat formula that pornography is 'sensation without feeling' while the erotic is 'feeling without sensation' - that is, the erotic is a mode of attention and knowledge that informs everything a woman does, from the making of a poem to the making of a bed. She illustrates with the difference between the demanding and the merely adequate in work, in friendship and in love; argues that the erotic is a measure of what we can ask of ourselves and others; and concludes that the erotic is a source of political power, because a woman who knows what satisfies her cannot be persuaded that she deserves less. The address is interrupted, in printed form, by its circumstances - it was delivered to an audience of historians of women - and its tone is the tone of the platform rather than the study. Its last movement turns from definition to obligation: to feel the erotic is to know what one can demand of oneself, and that knowledge is what makes political action possible.
narrative_structure: A spoken address in numbered sections, opening with a definition, moving through the distinction between the erotic and the pornographic, the account of what the erotic supplies to work and relationship, and the political conclusion; the paragraphs are short and declarative, and the argument advances by assertion and illustration rather than by citation.
meter_and_prosody: Direct address in the second person and the first person plural; short paragraphs with aphoristic closing sentences; a vocabulary that mixes the spiritual ('a deeply female and spiritual plane') with the political ('the erotic as power'); repetition and antithesis used as oral devices, as in the phrase that became its summary, 'pornography is sensation without feeling'.
historical_context: Delivered at the Fourth Berkshire Conference on the History of Women at Mount Holyoke College on 25 August 1978 and first published as a pamphlet by Out & Out Books; collected as the second essay in Sister Outsider: Essays and Speeches (Trumansburg, NY: Crossing Press, 1984). It belongs to the second wave's debates about sexuality and to the Black feminist critique of a feminism organised around white women's experience.
literary_significance: One of the founding documents of Black feminist thought and one of the most cited American essays of the period; it is a standard text in women's, gender and sexuality studies, it named the erotic as a political category, and it is the essay through which Lorde's thought is most often taught alongside 'The Master's Tools'.
bibliographical_notes: Delivered 25 August 1978; published as a pamphlet by Out & Out Books (1978) and later by Kore Press; collected in Sister Outsider: Essays and Speeches (1984) and in I Am Your Sister (2009). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The essay's central claim is that the erotic is a form of knowledge rather than a form of pleasure, and that the distinction between the erotic and the pornographic is the distinction between attention and consumption. From that follow its political claims: that women's distrust of their own satisfaction is a form of internalised oppression; that the energy of the erotic can be carried into work and politics; that the 'false belief that only the sexual is a proper source of power' keeps women divided from one another. The essay is also a link between the feminist and Black liberation arguments that Lorde made throughout Sister Outsider: the erotic is one of the resources with which difference can be lived rather than feared.
summary: A prose address in numbered sections in which Lorde argues that the erotic is a resource of deep knowledge and satisfaction that women have been taught to distrust, that it is not the same as the sexual and not the same as the pornographic, and that claiming it is a political act with consequences for work, friendship and love.
critical_context: Criticism reads the essay as a revaluation of a category that Western thought had placed below reason, as a contribution to the feminist ethics of pleasure, and as a text that complicates the period's debates between feminist anti-pornography and sex-radical positions; its relation to Audre Lorde's poetry of the same years, and to the tradition of Black women's writing about the body, has been widely discussed.
research_notes: The essay was read through the printed text in Sister Outsider as quoted in the sources consulted; the pamphlet's exact place and date of publication are given as the second-hand descriptions state them.

title: The Master's Tools Will Never Dismantle the Master's House
description: Comments delivered at the Second Sex Conference in New York on 29 September 1979 and printed in This Bridge Called My Back (1981) and in Sister Outsider (1984): an attack on a feminism that invites Black and lesbian women as tokens and a demand that difference be made the ground of political work.
plot_or_argument: Lorde speaks as a panellist at a conference marking thirty years of The Second Sex, and her remarks begin with the fact that the programme she has been invited to join has almost no Black women in it: the absence is the argument. She refuses the position of the token, describes the ways in which Black women and lesbians are asked to be present without being heard, and turns the conference's own subject - Beauvoir's account of woman as other - against it, pointing out that a feminism which makes the experience of white, middle-class, heterosexual women the measure of womanhood reproduces the structure it claims to oppose. Her central formulation is that the master's tools will never dismantle the master's house: the methods of a system cannot be used to end it. The address ends with a call to recognise difference - of race, sexuality, class and age - not as an obstacle to solidarity but as the material of it, and with the warning that a movement which cannot hear the difference within it will fail. The address is short - a few pages - and its force comes from the collision between the courtesy of the panel and the anger of the intervention: Lorde thanks the organisers and then tells them that their conference has reproduced the exclusions it denounces, and her own presence on the platform becomes the evidence for her argument.
narrative_structure: A short address in a handful of paragraphs, opening with the fact of exclusion, moving to the critique of the conference's theory, then to the general claim about tools and the house, and ending with a demand; the paragraphs are built as a sequence of assertions, and the last sentences are a warning and a promise.
meter_and_prosody: Direct, first-person, spoken prose with short declarative sentences and a few memorable formulations; anger held in formal syntax; the second person used to address the audience directly ('those of us who stand outside the circle of this society's definition of acceptable women'); no footnotes and no hedging.
historical_context: Delivered as comments at the 'Personal and the Political' panel of the Second Sex Conference at New York University on 29 September 1979, the conference marking the thirtieth anniversary of Beauvoir's The Second Sex; printed in This Bridge Called My Back: Writings by Radical Women of Color, ed. Cherrie Moraga and Gloria Anzaldua (1981), and in Sister Outsider (1984). It is one of the founding texts of intersectional feminism and of the Black feminist critique of the second wave.
literary_significance: One of the most quoted American essays of the twentieth century and a founding text of intersectionality; the sentence that gives it its title has become a proverb of political organising, the essay is a standard text in women's, gender and Black studies, and its argument about difference as the ground of solidarity shaped a generation of feminist theory.
bibliographical_notes: Delivered 29 September 1979; first printed in This Bridge Called My Back: Writings by Radical Women of Color, ed. Cherrie Moraga and Gloria Anzaldua (Watertown, MA: Persephone Press, 1981); collected in Sister Outsider: Essays and Speeches (1984). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The essay's argument is about the difference between inclusion and transformation: a conference, a movement or a theory that adds Black and lesbian women to an unchanged structure has not changed the structure. Lorde's terms are interlocking - race, class, sexuality and age are not separate oppressions to be ranked but a single complex reality - and her target is a white feminism that treats its own experience as universal. The essay is also a document of its occasion: the anger in it is directed at a particular room, and Lorde's insistence that anger is a source of information rather than a failure of civility became one of the most quoted arguments of Black feminist writing.
summary: A short address in which Lorde answers the organisers of a conference on Simone de Beauvoir, names the absence of Black and lesbian women from its programme, and argues that a movement cannot be liberated with the instruments of the system it opposes.
critical_context: Criticism reads the essay as the clearest statement of Lorde's theory of interlocking oppressions and as a key document in the history of the second wave's internal conflicts; its rhetoric, its use of the conference as a scene and its argument about anger have been widely analysed, and it is routinely taught with This Bridge Called My Back and with Kimberle Crenshaw's later work on intersectionality.
research_notes: The address was read through its printed text in the sources consulted; the date of delivery is given as the sources state it (29 September 1979), and the collection's own dating to 1979 in the anthology's list is consistent with it.

title: Against Interpretation
description: An essay published in the Evergreen Review in December 1964 and collected as the title essay of Against Interpretation (1966): Sontag argues that modern criticism has substituted the hunt for hidden meaning for the experience of art, and calls for an 'erotics' of art in place of a hermeneutics.
plot_or_argument: Sontag begins from a fact about the modern reader: that the first question asked of a work of art is what it means, and that interpretation - the translation of the visible into a hidden content - has become the dominant activity of criticism. She distinguishes two historical kinds of interpretation: the pre-modern kind, which sought to bring old texts up to date by allegory, and the modern kind, which she describes as 'excavating' and destroying, treating the work as a symptom of something the critic already knows (the Oedipal, the economic, the ideological). She argues that the modern style of interpretation has become a defensive response to the difficulty of modern art, a way of making it manageable; that it separates form from content, and that the separation is false; that the flight from interpretation is at the root of much of modern art's own difficulty; and that what is needed instead is a criticism that attends to the surface of works - to their descriptions, their textures, their ways of doing whatever they do. The essay's last sentences give the famous formula: 'In place of a hermeneutics we need an erotics of art.' The essay's method is to describe a habit of reading, give it a history, show what it costs, and propose a discipline in its place; its confidence comes from the assumption that criticism is a form of writing with its own pleasures, and its polemical edge from the conviction that most contemporary criticism had stopped looking at works of art altogether.
narrative_structure: An essay of some twenty pages in numbered sections, moving from description to history to polemic to prescription; the argument is carried by antithesis (form and content, depth and surface, hermeneutics and erotics) and ends with a compressed statement of aims rather than a conclusion.
meter_and_prosody: Aphoristic, confident, declarative prose with short paragraphs and frequent italicised terms; sentences built as definitions and reversals; a taste for lists and for the imperative; a first person plural that speaks for the age ('our culture', 'we are taught'), balanced by a critic's willingness to praise and blame particular works.
historical_context: First published in the Evergreen Review, vol. 8, no. 34 (December 1964), and collected as the opening essay of Against Interpretation and Other Essays (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1966), a finalist for the National Book Award; it belongs to Sontag's early New York period, when she was writing for the little magazines and the Partisan Review circle, and to the 1960s rethinking of criticism that produced the New Sensibility and the study of popular culture.
literary_significance: Among the most influential American essays of the century: it named a whole critical disposition, gave a generation its formula for describing works of art, and opened the way for the cultural studies and postcritique that followed; the essay is a standard text in courses on criticism and theory, and its closing phrase, 'an erotics of art', is one of the most quoted in modern criticism.
bibliographical_notes: First published in the Evergreen Review, vol. 8, no. 34 (December 1964); collected in Against Interpretation and Other Essays (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1966). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The essay's argument is about attention: to interpret a work in the modern manner is to replace it with a meaning that the critic already possessed, and so to lose the work's particularity. Sontag's alternative is descriptive rather than doctrinal - a criticism of form, of surface, of the sensuous life of works - and she connects it to the experience of contemporary art (abstract painting, the New Novel, the films of Bresson and Godard) in which the surface is not a veil over a meaning but the whole thing. The essay is also a document of the 1960s' argument with the New Criticism and with psychological and Marxist criticism, and of a moment when high and popular art began to be discussed in the same vocabulary.
summary: A prose essay in which Sontag describes the modern habit of interpretation, traces its history from the Greeks through Freud and Marx, argues that it has become a way of taming and diminishing art, and ends with a set of proposals for a criticism that would attend to the surface of works.
critical_context: Criticism has read the essay as the founding statement of a formalist and aestheticist criticism, as a transitional moment between the New Criticism and poststructuralism, and as a text whose influence on the 'postcritique' of the 2000s and 2010s has been acknowledged by its own originators; its relation to Robbe-Grillet's arguments for a 'poetics of presence', to camp and to the New Sensibility has all been discussed.
research_notes: The essay was read through the printed text and the sources consulted; quotations are short and confined to the sentences for which the essay is known.
